name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 1 May 1973

clue.text: For that matter grey can't be made white by indoctrination

blocks.note: grey matter is the stuff of the brain
laundering is what makes linen white

explanation.surface: A wry remark that a grey mind can never be scrubbed clean, however hard the propagandists work.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes that grey matter cannot be laundered white; read as wordplay, BRAIN (grey matter) is followed by WASHING (what makes things white), giving BRAINWASHING.
explanation.definitionFit: Brainwashing is forcible indoctrination, replacing a person's beliefs through pressure and repetition.

clue.text: They're all of a twitter, being a bit under par?

blocks.note: first meaning: birds twitter, and this is a child's word for little birds
second meaning: in golf, a hole completed in one stroke under par

explanation.walkthrough: 'All of a twitter' and 'under par' both sound like nervous, unwell people; one is birdsong and the other golf scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Small birds twitter, and in golf a birdie is a score of one stroke below par on a hole.

clue.text: A tartan type hat?

blocks.note: taken as written
tartan is the patterned cloth of Scotland, so its typical wearer is a Scot

explanation.surface: Asking whether a certain hat is the tartan kind, a tam-o'-shanter perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at a tam-o'-shanter; instead the Scot who wears tartan follows A.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot cap is a flat cloth hat, the style named after the Ascot racecourse where smart headwear is worn.

clue.text: Always thoughtless? Doesn't matter

definitions.note: a cryptic sense: never having a mind

blocks.note: first meaning, playful: at no time having a mind, that is, a mind never present
second meaning: the everyday phrase for dismissing something as unimportant

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical reading of the phrase, never plus mind, a mind absent at every moment; the question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'never mind' tells someone a thing is unimportant and not worth worrying about.

clue.text: Operatic affectations?

blocks.note: surface reading: the showy mannerisms of a prima donna
setter's reading: songs in an opera, and also pretentious manners

explanation.walkthrough: One word does both jobs: the arias of an opera are its songs, and putting on the same word means behaving affectedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Airs are melodies or songs, and 'airs and graces' are affected, superior manners.

clue.text: Whose misleading cases? The answer's fishy

definitions.note: asks whose: the answer is a family name used in the plural
an adjective defining a plural noun, fair because the clue says the answer itself is fishy, that is, consists of fish

blocks.note: first meaning: A. P. Herbert's comic 'Misleading Cases' stories star the litigant Albert Haddock
second meaning: the word is also the name of a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.walkthrough: A. P. Herbert's Misleading Cases were mock law reports in Punch, in which the perpetual litigant is Mr Albert Haddock. 'Fishy' sounds like suspicion, fitting the legal surface, but just means the answer names fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Haddock are cod-like food fish of the North Atlantic, and Haddock is also the litigant in Herbert's comic law cases.

clue.text: In the main a dirty low down spot

indicators.note: the answer lies in the words that follow, buried among their letters

blocks.note: running across the word boundaries of this phrase

explanation.surface: A dirty patch of sea down in the depths of the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is the open sea; the answer runs across the end of main, the word a, and the start of dirty. 'The' is filler between indicator and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, the point directly beneath an observer.

clue.text: Saint Robert Scot has one town in Ireland

blocks.note: ST is the usual abbreviation for saint
Rab is the Scottish short form of Robert
ane is the Scots word for one, the 'Scot' applying here too

explanation.surface: A Scottish saint called Robert owns a town in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scot' does double duty: it makes Robert into the Scottish RAB and one into the Scots ANE.
explanation.definitionFit: Strabane is a market town in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland, on the border with Donegal.

clue.text: Flung about fifty — what defence?

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word is placed round the second

blocks.note: to shy is to throw, so flung is shied
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone has thrown about fifty missiles: how will the defenders protect themselves?
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'approximately fifty', but it signals that one word goes round the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A shield is armour carried to ward off blows, the basic means of protection in battle.

clue.text: Gamp better?

blocks.note: a gamp is an umbrella, named after Dickens's Sarah Gamp
second meaning: well again after an illness

explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Gamp is a nurse in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, so the surface asks after a patient; her name also became slang for an umbrella, and an umbrella with new fabric is RE-COVERED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is better after an illness has recovered, and an umbrella fitted with a fresh canopy has been re-covered.

clue.text: Was Mrs Coster a Miss Hook?

definitions.note: adjective: the heroine is from Holland

blocks.note: first meaning: in cockney slang a man's wife is his 'old ...'
second meaning: Miss Hook of Holland is a 1907 musical comedy, so its heroine is from the Netherlands

explanation.walkthrough: A coster (costermonger) is a London street trader, and in cockney slang his wife is 'my old Dutch'. Miss Hook of Holland was a popular Edwardian musical, so Miss Hook is Dutch.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch is cockney slang for a wife and also the nationality of anyone from Holland.

clue.text: Is sending down under

blocks.note: surface reading: a convict being transported to Australia, the land 'down under'
setter's reading: lowering something below the ground, as at a burial

explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' looks like Australia and 'sending down' like a prison sentence; read literally it is putting a body down beneath the earth, which is what the answer does.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury a corpse, placing it down under the soil.

clue.text: For the relief of those who didn't make the good time

definitions.text: For the relief of those who didn't make the good time

blocks.clueFragment: those who didn't make the good time
blocks.note: surface reading: runners consoled after a slow race
setter's reading: a local tax levied to support people who never made good, the poor

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a slow time on the track, itself a pun on the answer read as 'a bad pace'; in fact it is the old parish tax that paid for relief of paupers, those who never made good.
explanation.definitionFit: The poor rate was the local levy in Britain that funded relief of paupers, people who had failed to prosper.

clue.text: Sally alters the image of the tories

indicators.note: changing the image of something reshapes it, so the following word is rearranged

blocks.note: the party name, used letter by letter

explanation.surface: A woman called Sally gives the Conservative party a makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: Sally looks like a woman's name heading a political story; it is the definition, in its military sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden attack made by troops from a besieged position, which is exactly a sortie.

clue.text: Author holds information put up by a turncoat

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means writing it bottom to top
a thing that holds another has it inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: Charles Reade, Victorian novelist of The Cloister and the Hearth
gen is informal British for information

explanation.surface: A writer protects secrets leaked to him by a defector.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN for information is British slang from wartime. Charles Reade is the author, and he holds the reversed NEG.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade is someone who deserts a cause or side for another, just as a turncoat does.

clue.text: Oblique and hairless horse

blocks.note: skew means slanting, at an angle
without hair

explanation.surface: A description of an odd-looking horse that is both lopsided and bald.
explanation.definitionFit: A skewbald is a horse with patches of white on a coat of another colour, other than black.

clue.text: Querying a goal can bring Hunter woe

indicators.note: the words can be brought round into another form, so their letters are reworked

blocks.note: the words used letter by letter

explanation.surface: Disputing a goal could land a player named Hunter in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a footballer protesting a goal; 'querying a goal' instead means asking to what end.
explanation.definitionFit: Whereunto is an old word asking for what purpose, so it questions the aim or goal of something.

clue.text: They're mean, and ladies may be loth to do so

definitions.text: ladies may be loth to do so
definitions.note: a cryptic sense: aver ages, declare their ages

blocks.note: first meaning: mean values in arithmetic

blocks.clueFragment: ladies may be loth to do so
blocks.note: second meaning, playful: to aver (declare) one's age is what a lady may avoid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like stingy, but it is the arithmetic sense. The second half splits the answer as AVER AGES, to declare how old one is, an old joke about ladies.
explanation.definitionFit: An average is the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers, so averages are means.

clue.text: Collared winger

blocks.note: surface reading: a football winger arrested, or grabbed by the collar
setter's reading: a bird with a ring of colour round its neck

explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a footballer and 'collared' an arrest, but a winger is anything with wings, and this pigeon wears a ring of feathers at the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The ring dove, or wood pigeon, has a pale band round its neck like a collar, and it is a bird, a creature of wings.

clue.text: Come along, Sisyphus!

definitions.note: an instruction to Sisyphus, a verb phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: the showman's cry inviting a crowd to gather
second meaning: what Sisyphus is condemned to do with his boulder for eternity

explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Sisyphus must forever push a boulder uphill, so the command he hears is to push it up the slope; the same phrase is a fairground barker's invitation.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Roll up!' is the barker's call urging people to come along, and rolling the stone up is Sisyphus's endless punishment.

clue.text: League fittings in boots?

blocks.note: surface reading: fixtures, the scheduled matches of a sporting league
setter's reading: the number that fits before 'league' to name the fairytale boots

explanation.walkthrough: In the fairytale, seven-league boots cover seven leagues at a stride; the plural answer is what fits in front of 'league' to name them.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairytale footwear are seven-league boots, so the number seven is what is fitted to 'league' in their name.

clue.text: Artful tinker goes round the gallery looking grand

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so the gallery ends up inside

blocks.note: an artful, crafty tinker is a sly one
the Tate is the famous London art gallery

explanation.surface: A crafty tinker strolls through an art gallery looking very dignified.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's national gallery of British and modern art.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately means dignified and imposing, with the impressive bearing of something grand.

clue.text: Fire-vessels?

blocks.note: surface reading: fireboats or braziers, vessels that hold or fight fire
setter's reading: things that start a fire, and also flat barges used to unload ships

explanation.walkthrough: The word for small devices that kindle flames is also the word for barges that ferry cargo from ship to shore, so one word covers both halves of the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: Lighters kindle fires, and a lighter is also a flat-bottomed boat, a working vessel in a harbour.

clue.text: Trunk addressed to rail way sorting office

blocks.note: taken as written
R.S.O. was the postal abbreviation for a railway sorting office

explanation.surface: A travelling trunk labelled for despatch to the railway's postal sorting office.
explanation.walkthrough: Old postal addresses could end with R.S.O., a railway sorting office; the label on the trunk reads TO followed by those initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the trunk of the human body, the part apart from head and limbs.

clue.text: Let Eva twirl in the dance

indicators.note: to twirl is to spin round, so the letters are spun into a new order

blocks.note: the words used letter by letter

explanation.surface: An invitation to let a woman called Eva spin round on the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The veleta is an old-time ballroom dance in waltz rhythm, popular in Britain early in the twentieth century.

clue.text: Sends out for this paper perhaps

indicators.note: out suggests being put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the newspaper printing this crossword was The Canberra Times

explanation.surface: Someone sends out for a copy of this newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue appeared in The Canberra Times, so 'this paper' is the Times, and 'perhaps' admits the indirection.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to send something forth, as a lamp gives off light or a chimney sends up smoke.

clue.text: The churchwarden is but mortal

blocks.note: first meaning: a churchwarden is a long-stemmed pipe made of fired earthenware
second meaning: the earthly substance of the human body

explanation.walkthrough: A churchwarden looks like a parish official, a fitting subject for a sermon on mortality, but it is also a long tobacco pipe made of fired earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Clay is the material of a churchwarden pipe and, in biblical language, the stuff mortal humans are made from.

clue.text: Inundated Neath

definitions.note: an adjective defining an adverb, fair because inundated land lies under, that is, below the water

blocks.note: first meaning: flooded, lying beneath water
second meaning: 'neath is a poetic short form of beneath

explanation.walkthrough: Neath is also a town in South Wales, so the surface reads as news of a flood; here it is the poetic preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Neath means below, and something inundated is below the water's surface.

clue.text: That's dished the girl Anne surrounding it in reverse

indicators.note: going in reverse means read backwards, from last letter to first
one word surrounding another puts it around the other, the second sitting inside

blocks.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
the name taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl called Anne has been jilted, lost in a daydream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dished' looks like slang for being let down, but it means served up on a plate. The container works on the reversed word only, before the girl's piece is set in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A galantine is a cold dish of boned, stuffed meat in aspic, so it is something served up on a plate.

clue.text: Call of those on Council waiting lists? It's a gamble

definitions.text: Call of those on Council waiting lists?

blocks.clueFragment: Call of those on Council waiting lists?
blocks.note: first meaning, playful: people waiting for a council flat calling out for a home
second meaning: an old name for the numbers game now called bingo

explanation.walkthrough: Council housing is public rented housing in Britain, with long waiting lists, so its applicants might cry out for a home. The answer was also the call of the winner, and the game's name, in what is now bingo.
explanation.definitionFit: Housey-housey is the old British name for bingo, a game of chance played for money.
